summary:
We developed LITTLE MARSONAUT, a Mars base simulation game designed for children to learn about space science through interactive gameplay.
The goal is to survive on Mars for as many days as possible while collecting valuable geological samples and conducting scientific research. Players must optimize limited resources, including electricity, water, oxygen, and food, while balancing survival and exploration.
The game features interactive mini-games for solar energy collection and tomato growing, as well as resource conversion through water electrolysis and underground water ice extraction. Changing Martian weather conditions create different challenges each time, affecting resource management and rover missions.
Players can send Curiosity Jr. to explore Mars, where each mission may uncover different geological samples and real Mars photos taken by NASA's Curiosity rover. Rare discoveries may even lead to an early, successful return to Earth for further research.
By combining scientific knowledge, strategic decisions, and engaging gameplay, we aim to spark children's curiosity about space exploration and make science more accessible and enjoyable.
details:
How It Works

LITTLE MARSONAUT is a browser-based Mars survival and exploration game designed for children aged 7–12.

Players manage a small Mars base while trying to survive for as many days as possible and collect valuable geological samples for scientific research.

The game focuses on four essential resources: electricity, water, oxygen, and food. Players must decide how to use these limited resources while balancing the needs of the base with scientific exploration.

Simulated Martian weather conditions, including dust storms and radiation hazards, affect solar energy collection and rover missions. If an essential resource runs out, the mission ends early.

Game Features

The Mars base has four main areas:

  • Base Center: Check simulated Martian weather conditions, review collected geological samples, and view real NASA Mars mission images.
  • Rover Garage: Send Curiosity Jr. on exploration missions. Players can choose how much electricity to use for each expedition. Dust storms and radiation hazards may damage the rover, requiring repairs before another mission.
  • Greenhouse: Grow tomatoes by watering plants and using electricity for lighting and temperature control. Players must harvest tomatoes when they are ripe to maintain their food supply.
  • Power Lab: Collect solar energy through an interactive mini-game, produce oxygen through water electrolysis, and extract underground water ice using electricity.

Game Strategy & Mission Outcomes

Resource Management

Players need to balance survival and exploration. For example, using more electricity for a rover mission leaves less power for growing food or producing oxygen. They must also decide whether to use electricity for water ice extraction or other essential activities.

Unpredictable Exploration

Each rover mission can produce different results. Players may collect common rocks, discover rare geological samples, or return without finding anything. The results depend on the game's exploration mechanics and environmental conditions.

Mission Failure

If an essential resource runs out, the crew must end its Mars research mission and return to Earth.

Special Scientific Discovery

Under rare conditions, players may discover a geological sample with significant scientific potential. This triggers a special successful ending in which the crew returns to Earth early so the sample can be studied further.

Educational Benefits

We wanted children to learn about space science by making decisions and interacting with the environment rather than simply reading information.

The game introduces several scientific ideas:

  • Space Science: Players can read short science facts during waiting periods or click the "?" buttons to learn about Mars, space farming, and exploration. These explanations include NASA images and links to official resources.
  • Space Exploration Risks: Dust storms, radiation hazards, and limited resources introduce some of the challenges that future astronauts may face on Mars.
  • Resource Conversion: Players learn how electricity and water can be used to produce oxygen through electrolysis, and how extracting water ice requires energy.
  • Mars Geology: Rover missions introduce different types of Martian rocks and minerals.
  • Learning Through Simulation: Players experience how decisions about limited resources can affect the survival and progress of a Mars mission.

The environmental conditions, resource consumption, and rover discoveries are simulated for gameplay. They are not presented as actual daily measurements or exploration results from Mars.

NASA Data and Scientific Resources

We integrated the NASA Image and Video Library API to display real Mars mission images and the NASA DONKI Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) API to retrieve information about solar activity.

The game also includes 25 short science facts based on NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources. These cover topics such as Mars geology, rover exploration, solar storms, space farming, and astronaut life.

We use these resources to connect the game's activities with real scientific knowledge. For example, NASA space weather information provides context for the simulated radiation hazards, while official Mars imagery helps players see what the planet actually looks like.

Players can also follow links to NASA resources if they want to learn more about a topic.

Creativity & Innovation

One of our main ideas was to combine resource management with exploration.

Players cannot focus only on keeping the base running or only on collecting geological samples. They need to balance both goals, since exploration requires electricity and environmental hazards can affect the rover.

We also wanted each playthrough to feel different. Changing simulated weather, unexpected rover discoveries, and resource trade-offs encourage players to try different strategies.

The rare discovery ending adds another possibility beyond simply surviving for as long as possible. It gives players an additional scientific goal to work toward.

Design Considerations

Target Audience

We designed the game for children aged 7–12. We wanted the activities and instructions to be easy to understand without removing the scientific ideas behind them.

Engagement

Interactive mini-games, changing environmental conditions, and different rover discoveries help make the experience more engaging and encourage repeated play.

Scientific Accuracy

We used NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources as references while simplifying some scientific concepts for gameplay. We also distinguish between real NASA data and simulated game conditions.

Accessibility

The game runs directly in a web browser and does not require installation. We used illustrated environments, simple controls, and short explanations to make it approachable for younger players.

Tools & Technologies

  • HTML, CSS, and Tailwind CSS: Website structure, interface design, and animations.
  • JavaScript and React: Game logic, resource calculations, exploration probabilities, and interactive components.
  • SVG: Mars base illustrations and interactive graphics.
  • NASA Image and Video Library API: Real Mars mission imagery.
  • NASA DONKI SEP API: Solar energetic particle event data used as a reference for simulated space weather hazards.
  • GitHub: Version control and team collaboration.
    • link： https://github.com/Nadia-tomato/little-marsonaut
  • Render: Website deployment and hosting.

Intended Impact

We hope LITTLE MARSONAUT can make space science more interesting and accessible to children.

By managing resources, exploring Mars, and encountering unexpected challenges, players can gain a better understanding of what future Mars missions might involve.

Most importantly, we want the game to encourage curiosity. Through interactive learning and links to real NASA resources, children can continue exploring scientific topics beyond the game itself.
